newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec reinforces use of French in the workplace.
newsitem.headline: Quebec reinforces use of French in the workplace.

text.p: Quebec said on Thursday that it will no longer subsidize or award contracts to companies operating in Quebec that do not have a certificate of francization from the provincial government.

The certificates are awarded by the government's Office de la langue francaise to companies meeting all existing requirements on the use of the French language in the workplace. The measure targets businesses with more than 50 employees.
Government agencies will also have to respect the new rules.
The measures were announced as part of the Parti Quebecois government's plan to reinforce the use of French in Quebec.

"The government must set the example. Quebec is not bilingual, it is unilingually French," Culture and Communications Minister Louise Beaudoin told reporters after announcing measures to curb the use of French in the civil service.
She said Quebec will also require companies seeking government subsidies or contracts to prepare their documents in French only.
Of the province's more than 7 million population, about 83 percent are French-speaking. French has been Quebec's official language since 1974.

In 1977, shortly after the separatist Parti Quebecois was elected to its first-ever mandate, Quebec enacted Bill 101, The Charter of the French Language, a controversial piece of legislation that eliminated the use of English on commercial signs and restricted access to English schooling for certain residents.
